Annual Meetings

Morning Session - 2017 Meeting

Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger discuss Berkshire's big investment in Wells Fargo in light of the bank's "fake accounts" scandal. Buffett also explains why he sold a big chunk of IBM stock while buying Apple shares, and changed his mind on airlines.

Sat, May 6 2017 • 9:00 AM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 6. Wells Fargo didn't act quickly enough to stop bad behavior
  2. 12. Making mistakes with IBM, Google, and Amazon
  3. 13. Buffett defends investing in competitive airline industry
  4. 23. Big change: You don't need money to run America's biggest companies
  5. 31. "If the board hires a compensation consultant after I go, I will come back"
  6. 34. Most financial advisors don't deserve their fees

Sync Video to Paragraph

At Wells Fargo, you know, there were three very significant mistakes, but there was one that dwarfs all of the others.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You're going to have incentive systems at any business â almost any business. There's nothing wrong with incentive systems, but you've got to be very careful what you incentivize. And you can't incentivize bad behavior. And if so, you better have a system for recognizing it.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Clearly, at Wells Fargo, there was an incentive system built around the idea of cross-selling and number of services per customer. And the company, in every quarterly investor presentation, highlighted how many services per customer. So, it was the focus of the organization â a major focus.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And undoubtedly, people got paid and graded and promoted based on that number â at least partly based on that number.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

We've made similar mistakes. I mean any company's going to make some mistakes in designing a system.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

But the biggest mistake was that â and I don't know â obviously don't know all the facts as to how the information got passed up the line at Wells Fargo.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But at some point, if there's a major problem, the CEO will get wind of it. And that is â at that moment, that's the key to everything, because the CEO has to act.

Sync Video to Paragraph

That Salomon situation that you saw happened because of â on April, I think, 28th, the CEO of Salomon, the president of Salomon, the general counsel of Salomon, sat in a room and they had described to them, by a fellow named John Meriwether, some bad practice, terrible practice, that was being conducted by a fellow named Paul Mozer, who worked for them.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And Paul Mozer was flimflamming the United States Treasury, which is a very dumb thing to do. And he was doing it partly out of spite, because he didn't like the Treasury and they didn't like him. So he put in phony bids for U.S. Treasurys and all of that.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So on April 28th, roughly, the CEO and all these people knew that they had something that had gone very wrong, and they had to report it to the Federal Reserve Board in New York â the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We look â to get to your question, Jonny â we look for taking the longer maturity situations. We always have.

Sync Video to Paragraph
